# Agent Notes

An Agent Note is a durable decision record: the *why* and the *what was given up* that code, tests and ordinary documentation cannot carry. It survives the session that produced it; a later session or maintainer can recover the rationale instead of re-litigating it.

This skill owns the full lifecycle of those records — where they live, when to write one, the uniform format, how they move and are pruned, and how finished ones are frozen into an archive. The references hold the full rules; the bundled script decides the mechanical ones.

For substantial future work, a proposed note owns the design while the project's execution tracker owns status and evidence. A proposal becomes active guidance only after it enters the target branch's `proposed/` inventory; approval or merge of a proposal is not implementation.

## Defaults

Apply this skill's use-site default only when neither the request nor existing project instructions choose one. Treat existing instructions as authoritative read-only input; do not ask for, create, modify, or copy instructions merely to select a default.

## Procedure

1. **Route substantial future work.** Load [the workflow contract](references/workflow.md) and [the notes contract](references/notes-contract.md) before deciding whether substantial future work needs a proposal, linking its execution tracker, or checkpointing implementation. A proposal that exists only on a working branch, Draft change or unmerged branch is not active inventory. Create or find the design owner and execution tracker before implementation, and do not treat a branch-local proposal as approval.
2. **Check supersession before writing.** Search the active tree for notes that own or constrain the same decision. Use the project's current code, configuration, package documentation, generated catalogs, newer notes and inbound links to establish whether an older rationale still owns or constrains anything. Plan one change for every match: update the owner, consolidate a full supersession, archive a qualifying implemented note, or reject or delete a stale proposal. A new note never competes with an existing owner.
3. **Initialize the tree once.** In a project that has none, run `node <skill-dir>/scripts/notes.mjs init` before the first note. It creates the lifecycle and class folders and the six archived class folders with ignored `.gitkeep` placeholders only in empty folders, and never overwrites an existing file.
4. **Choose the lifecycle.** Substantial future work starts in `proposed/`; a decision already made starts in `implemented/`; a declined proposal goes to `rejected/` with the reason on its status line. The loaded notes contract owns the path, format, classification, companion and pruning rules for creating, updating, reviewing, auditing, moving, consolidating or pruning a note.
5. **Keep an implemented note true.** Update paths, names, keys and defaults in the same change that alters them, and rewrite stale facts in place; do not append a change history. That tracks realization, not the decision: a reversed decision needs a new note that supersedes the old one.
6. **Checkpoint implementation.** Keep a proposal in `proposed/` while any accepted criterion or goal remains unshipped. The execution tracker records completed and pending evidence; the note does not become a progress log. Move the note only when its accepted scope has shipped and its verification is recorded. The workflow contract owns full and partial checkpoints, multi-goal scope and commit evidence.
7. **Prune as part of the change**, never as a separate word-count or age sweep. The keep, archive, reject or delete decision is semantic and follows the notes contract.
8. **Run the checks.** Load [the notes contract](references/notes-contract.md#companions) before auditing so the project's companion mechanism is known. Run `node <skill-dir>/scripts/notes.mjs check` with every declared companion option; for example, a project whose units use `.zh.md` translations and `.i18n.yaml` records runs `check --companion .zh.md --companion .i18n.yaml`. A bare check is valid only when the project declares no companions. `check` fails when the active tree has no notes. Run `node <skill-dir>/scripts/notes.mjs archive` for the frozen archive; archive verification fails when no artifact is sealed. A change that leaves a failing check is unfinished. `<skill-dir>` stands for this skill directory; the project's own suite may wrap the commands.

## Where notes live

The root defaults to `.agents/dsh-spec-agent-notes/` directly under the project root, the Git checkout root of the working directory. The project's standing instructions (`AGENTS.md` or the file it cites) may name another root inside the project. The archive root is always `<notes root>/archived`. The notes contract owns the closed lifecycle and class trees, filenames and links.

## Writing the note

Write a note only for lasting decision rationale that code, tests and existing documentation do not explain. Update the note that owns the decision instead of creating a duplicate. Mechanical or local edits, including local UI presentation and interaction changes, are exempt. A note is never edited into a different decision: supersede it with a new one and keep both cross-linked unless the old note is later consolidated into its owner.

The notes contract owns the header, status lines, required sections and alternatives rule. A note that changes lifecycle moves to that lifecycle's path and satisfies its format in the same change.

For a substantial future proposal, the workflow contract owns the relationship between the note, its execution tracker and implementation evidence. Retaining the proposal still leaves it `proposed/`; implementation checkpoints decide when the shipped decision may move.

## Companions

A unit is a note plus every companion the project assigns to it. Companions may be translations, records, diagrams or other support. An external mechanism owns names, formats and checks and determines the companion set; Agent Notes owns the declared unit's grouping, movement and sealing. Installing a mechanism alone neither enables nor makes it available.

When translation is available, choose this note's target set in this order:

1. the current request;
2. existing project instructions;
3. a consistent target set from complete pairs in the same owner-defined class;
4. the primary agent's user language, when it differs from the source language;
5. no translation companion.

The model judges comparable files and project evidence; scripts receive resolved companion facts. A target set may contain several languages. Translation requires project evidence and availability; missing or conflicting evidence selects none without asking.

Adding a target is progressive: new notes use the current set, edited notes gain missing targets, and untouched notes do not change. Removing a target clears every eligible active and unsealed unit; sealed units stay frozen. Before producing any translation companion, apply the translation mechanism's working-separation rule. When no isolated or otherwise verifiable separation is available, finish the source note and hand off the selected target without translating in the working context. Failure leaves the unit unfinished with source, target, failed step and next step; it never becomes English-only. The [notes contract](references/notes-contract.md#companions) owns full rules. Use the project's translation mechanism (when available, use the dsh-spec-translate-docs skill).

## Archiving

Only an `implemented/` note may enter. Load [the archive contract](references/archive-contract.md) before archiving; it owns the archive path, units, six class directories and seal rules.

Finish selected companions and owner checks while the note is active; failure leaves it active and unfinished. Move the complete unit, add the archive metadata and re-record companions through the archive contract. A new unit with any companion requires an owner readiness command; omission fails preparation and leaves the manifest unchanged. Before sealing, prepare the final membership, hashes and required owner checks; run `archive --write` with the matching plan only when the prepared unit is unchanged and every readiness check passed, then stage and verify. A successful manifest write is the freeze boundary. When readiness fails, report the failing command and output, keep the unit unsealed and the manifest unchanged, then tell the operator to repair the named condition and rerun `archive --prepare` before using a new plan with `archive --write`.

Once sealed, a unit is permanently frozen: never edit, update, move, translate, reformat or delete it, and never add or remove a companion. It is not authority for current behavior; new decisions and facts belong in an active note or current documentation, and documentation gates skip archived sources, including their outbound links. The archive's structure and hashes live in `<root>/archived/manifest.json`, append-only against the baseline at the manifest's project-relative path. [The archive contract](references/archive-contract.md#the-frozen-guarantee) owns the full guarantee.

The archive contract owns the prepare, readiness and guarded-write commands and the Git baseline requirement.

## Checks

Run `init`, `check` and `archive` from inside the project's Git checkout. Before `check`, load the notes contract's companion section and pass the project's declared suffixes and format options. Before `archive`, load the archive contract. The gate checks the active tree or frozen archive, and a failing state is unfinished work. `--help` lists each command's options and exit codes. The model judges whether a note should exist and whether its rationale still guides work; the script decides the mechanical facts owned by the loaded contract.

## Stop and hand over

Stop and report rather than guess when:

- a sealed artifact is missing, changed, or not covered by the manifest;
- the archive baseline cannot be trusted — rewritten history without an external `--base-ref`, a baseline commit that cannot be read, or no Git repository — or the root, archive root or manifest resolves outside the project root after symlinks are followed, or inside the project's Git directory, or the archive root does not belong to the project's Git directory; or the manifest lists artifacts but is not tracked by Git in the project (stage or commit the seal before verifying); or a bare repository (no worktree) is the project root;
- the note's class, lifecycle or owning decision is unclear;
- a change would reverse a decision or repair frozen history.

Every handover names the failed step, completed work, pending work and a resumable recovery action. A failed archive readiness check leaves the unit unsealed and the manifest unchanged; name the failing check and the project's next command, such as repairing the named condition and rerunning `archive --prepare` before `archive --write`. A reversed decision becomes a new note; restoring a sealed unit or repairing a damaged archive is a handover, not a rewrite.

## References

- [Proposal-first workflow](references/workflow.md) — load before routing substantial future work, linking its execution tracker, checkpointing implementation, or moving a completed proposal to `implemented/`.
- [Notes contract](references/notes-contract.md) — load before writing, moving, consolidating or pruning a note.
- [Archive contract](references/archive-contract.md) — load before archiving, sealing or verifying the archive.

# Proposal-first workflow

This contract owns how substantial future work moves from design through execution and into an implemented Agent Note. [The notes contract](notes-contract.md) owns the active tree, note format, classification, companions, supersession and pruning; [the archive contract](archive-contract.md) owns frozen history.

The notes contract decides whether the work needs a durable record. This contract applies when it does, or when an existing proposal or execution tracker already governs the work.

## One owner for each fact

| Artifact | Owns | Does not own |
|---|---|---|
| Proposed Agent Note | Problem, intended change, alternatives, acceptance criteria and risks | Execution status or commit history |
| Execution issue or tracker item | Dependencies, status, completed and pending evidence, next checkpoint and links | Rationale, alternatives or a second copy of the complete design |
| Implementation commit or change request | The code, configuration, documentation and tests actually shipped, with their verification | A mutable design or execution status |

Each proposal links its execution tracker, and each tracker item links back to its proposal. The tracker may summarize the outcome needed for execution, but the proposal remains the authority for the complete design and acceptance criteria.

Use one proposal and one tracker item for a coherent decision. Split independent decisions into separate proposals and tracker items rather than using one proposal as a project plan or one issue as a design document.

## Retain the proposal before implementation

Before design or implementation of substantial future work:

1. Search the target branch's active `proposed/` inventory for a note that owns or constrains the decision. Search by the problem, mechanism and rejected alternatives, not only by a proposed title.
2. A note confined to a working tree, Draft change, unmerged branch or stale local revision is not active inventory. It may inform discussion, but it is not authority for implementation and cannot be resumed as though it had been retained.
3. When no retained owner exists, write one proposed note under the project's notes root and associate one tracker item. The note links that item; the item links the note's path and records execution status. If the proposal needs translation or another companion, complete the selected unit before retaining it.
4. Retain the design before implementation. A proposal-only change is reviewed and merged with `Status: proposed` under `proposed/`; approval of the design does not change its lifecycle. If review changes the decision, alternatives or accepted scope, update the proposal before implementation relies on it.
5. Start implementation from the proposal present in the target inventory. If the target branch, tracker or proposal mechanism cannot be inspected, hand over the missing discoverability step rather than treating a draft as retained.

This gate does not turn small mechanical or local work into a proposal. The notes contract's write trigger still decides whether a durable record is owed.

## Record execution evidence

An implementation commit or change request performs the work and names the execution tracker through the project's convention. A partial change uses the project's non-closing reference convention and leaves the tracker status explicit; a closing or resolving reference is reserved for a change that satisfies the tracked scope. The tracker records the evidence a later session needs to resume: which accepted criterion the change completed, which commit or change request carries it, what verification ran, and what remains.

Do not create a work record, a progress diary, per-criterion proposals, or another status store. A project decision that removed a prior work record may define a measured condition for reintroducing it; honor that condition. Without that condition, Git history and the execution tracker preserve implementation history, the proposal preserves the design, and a commit message states what shipped without becoming the live status owner.

## Checkpoint full and partial work

Checkpoint after each material implementation goal, before declaring the work complete, and whenever work pauses or resumes:

1. Read the current proposal and tracker from the target inventory.
2. Compare every acceptance criterion with the implementation actually shipped and its verification evidence.
3. Keep the note in `proposed/` if any accepted criterion, goal or required companion remains incomplete. Record the completed evidence and the next pending outcome in the tracker.
4. If implementation reveals a factual path, name or mechanism change, update the proposal's current facts and its companions. A change to the decision, alternatives or accepted scope is a design change and returns to proposal review before implementation proceeds from it.
5. Move the note to `implemented/` only at the complete checkpoint: every accepted criterion is shipped and verified, and the implemented skeleton and companions are satisfied in the same change. Update the tracker link to the implemented path.
6. When work is abandoned, reject or delete the proposal under the notes contract. Do not leave an obsolete proposal as an implicit backlog item.

Completion is not a count of commits. A partial implementation with one completed goal and one pending goal remains `proposed/`; a complete implementation with all accepted goals closed moves to `implemented/`.

## Multi-goal proposals

A coherent proposal may have several acceptance criteria or several execution-tracker goals. Track each goal's evidence in the tracker, and evaluate the proposal's lifecycle against the complete accepted set.

- If any accepted goal is unfinished, the note remains `proposed/`.
- If accepted goals are delivered in separate changes, checkpoint each change and keep the remaining goals visible.
- If a partial delivery is itself an independent, complete decision, it may receive its own implemented note while the broader proposal remains proposed and cross-linked. A subset of the same decision keeps the single proposed owner.
- If scope is reduced or expanded, update the proposal's acceptance criteria and review that design change before using the new scope to declare completion.
- Do not silently treat an unfinished goal as delivered because another goal in the same proposal shipped.

## Move the owner

Moving a proposal to `implemented/` is one lifecycle change: use the implemented status and skeleton, keep the first-proposed filename date, move the complete unit, re-record companions, and update the tracker and inbound links. The notes contract owns the format and the archive contract owns later archiving.

## Do not copy standing instructions

This workflow does not create or modify `AGENTS.md`, a generated policy file, or another standing-instruction asset. The installed skill and the project's existing instructions supply the rule; a project names only its notes root and repository conventions where those values differ.

## Report a checkpoint

Report the design owner and status, the execution tracker, the evidence for each completed goal, the remaining accepted goals, and the relevant notes and companion checks. A full checkpoint also reports the new implemented path and updated links.

# Agent Notes contract

Agent Notes are effectively RFCs written by agents: durable proposals and decision records that preserve the rationale, the alternatives, the consequences and the required verification that code, tests and ordinary documentation cannot carry. They exist so a later session can find out why a decision was made and what it beat before it re-opens the question.

This contract owns the active lifecycle tree, while [the workflow contract](workflow.md) owns the proposal/issue/commit split, target-inventory discoverability, retention as proposed and execution checkpoints. [The archive contract](archive-contract.md) owns the frozen archive; [SKILL.md](../SKILL.md) owns the procedure.

## Layout and naming

Every note has two axes, both encoded in its path — `{lifecycle}/{class}/yyyy-mm-dd-topic-title.md`:

- **Lifecycle** (the top-level folder) is the note's status, and a note moves between folders as its status changes:
  - **`proposed/`** — proposals reviewed before implementation; not yet built, or only partly.
  - **`implemented/`** — the decision shipped. The file records what was decided and what was rejected, and is kept current with what actually shipped: when code later moves a file, renames a package, or changes a key, default or mechanism, the note is updated in the same change to match. Rewrite the stale fact in place; do not append a change history.
  - **`rejected/`** — the proposal was considered and declined. Keep it only while its rationale prevents a tempting, meaningful mistake; otherwise delete the complete unit.
- **Class** (the nested folder) is the kind of decision — see [Classification](#classification).

The date in the filename is when the topic was first proposed, per the project's history. Cross-references between notes use relative Markdown links (`[topic](../../implemented/architecture/2026-…-….md)`) — never bare prose or numbers — so they are mechanically checkable and survive moves between folders.

The active lifecycle tree is the working inventory: browse its lifecycle and class folders or search the project. Do not add a centralized `INDEX.md`: it duplicates path metadata and makes unrelated note changes contend on one file. Implemented records with historical decision value but little future guidance move to the separate frozen [archive](archive-contract.md).

Read the project's standing instructions (`AGENTS.md` or the file it cites) for the notes root. The default is `.agents/dsh-spec-agent-notes/` directly under the project root, which is the Git checkout root of the working directory; the directory is the notes tree itself, with the lifecycle folders and `archived/` inside it. Every command accepts `--root <dir>` for another directory inside the project root; the archive root is always `<notes root>/archived`. Run `node <skill-dir>/scripts/notes.mjs init` once in a project without a tree: it creates the lifecycle and class folders and the six archived class folders with ignored `.gitkeep` placeholders in empty folders, and never overwrites an existing file. Commit the initialized skeleton before the first seal, because the archive baseline is read from Git.

## Classification

Every note has one class, encoded in its path; the classification gate rejects other folders that hold Markdown. An empty directory is ignored, as the source's Markdown glob never sees it. Adding a class is a deliberate change: extend the table below and the gate's closed set in the same change.

| Class | What it covers |
|---|---|
| `feature` | A new user- or model-facing capability. |
| `bug-fix` | Corrects a defect or closes a gap a postmortem surfaced. |
| `simplification` | Removes code, behavior, or surface area without adding a capability. |
| `architecture` | A structural decision about the **shipped source** — how packages relate, what the runtime vocabulary is. |
| `process` | Tooling, policy, or workflow **around** the code — gates, the package manager, vendoring — not runtime behavior. |
| `testing` | Test infrastructure and strategy. |

The `architecture` / `process` line: **architecture** is about the source the project ships; **process** is the surrounding tooling and workflow. A `refactor` class is deliberately absent — it overlaps `simplification`, whose discriminator ("does observable behavior change?") already covers it. The six names and definitions are the upstream set, unchanged; a general-domain agent maps its own work onto them semantically: `feature` for a new capability, `bug-fix` for a correction, `simplification` for a removal, `architecture` for a structural decision, `process` for the surrounding workflow, `testing` for acceptance and verification. When no class fits exactly, choose the closest intent; adding a class is a contract and gate change, never an improvised folder. The gate does not second-guess that mapping.

The gate rejects any other folder that holds Markdown; an empty directory is not a note folder. A project that genuinely needs a class adds it here and in the gate; it does not improvise a folder.

## When to write one

Write or update the owning note only for lasting decision rationale that code, tests and existing documentation do not explain; the note is part of that change. A proposal for substantial future work starts in `proposed/`; a decision already made starts in `implemented/`. Pick the class that matches the decision. A branch-local proposal is not active inventory; the workflow contract owns retention and execution-tracker linkage.

**Every new note triggers a supersession check.** Search the active tree for older notes covering the same decision, mechanism or rejected alternative, and classify each match while writing the new note: update the owner, consolidate a full supersession, archive a qualifying implemented unit, reject an obsolete proposal, or delete a rejection that no longer prevents a mistake. Keep partial supersessions active and cross-linked. Do not defer a known match to a later corpus audit.

Updating the note that already owns the decision satisfies the rule; do not create a duplicate. Mechanical or local edits, including local UI presentation and interaction changes, are exempt. A note is never edited into a *different* decision: supersede it with a new one and keep both notes cross-linked unless the old note is later fully consolidated under this rule. Editing an `implemented/` note to track where its existing decision lives is required, not forbidden.

An implemented note that is fully superseded may be consolidated into the current owning note and deleted. Before deletion the owner must preserve every unique rationale, alternative, consequence, required verification and named coverage gap; repair every inbound link; and delete the old note and its companions in the same change. Partial supersession does not qualify: keep both notes cross-linked and update every fact that remains current. Consolidation must not rewrite the old file into its opposite or rely on the project's history as the only copy of the rationale.

A feature-addition note may be consolidated into a later removal note only when the feature is absent from production code, configuration, schemas, durable or wire formats, migration and compatibility behavior; no current documentation presents it as available; and no test exercises it as supported behavior. Removal rationale and tests that verify absence may remain. The removal owner preserves the original motivation, why it no longer justified the feature, alternatives to full removal, the capability given up, conditions for reintroduction, and verification of complete absence. Obsolete implementation inventories and tests that only verified the deleted behavior are not current verification evidence. Removing one transport, default, implementation or presentation is partial supersession, as is any surviving durable data or compatibility handling.

## The file format

Every active note follows one in-file format, and the bundled gate enforces it. Archived notes retain the format they had when sealed, plus the archive-date line immediately below the `Status: implemented` line.

### The header block

The first three lines of every note are exactly:

```markdown
# Agent Note: <title>

Status: <status>
```

followed by a blank line. The `Status:` value is one of three forms and must agree with the lifecycle folder:

- `Status: proposed`
- `Status: implemented`
- `Status: rejected — <why, in one line>`

The status carries no dates and no parentheticals: the filename holds the first-proposed date, the project's history holds everything else, and an "accepted in amended form" note is body content (state the amendment where the decision is stated). The rejection reason is the one status with content, because a rejected note's verdict is the fact readers come for.

The gate requires the header lines and exactly one `Status:` line in prose.

### The body skeleton

Every note opens its body with `## Problem` — the motivation, written to stand without the solution. What follows depends on the lifecycle; recurring sections use these canonical names and nothing else, while genuinely bespoke technical sections remain free-form between the required ones.

#### `proposed/`

```markdown
## Problem
## Proposal
…bespoke sections…
## Alternatives considered
## Acceptance criteria
## Risks
```

`## Proposal` is the intended change and may legitimately speak in the future tense — plans, migration steps and open questions belong here while the work is unbuilt. `## Acceptance criteria` says what observable state means done. `## Risks` covers both what could go wrong and what the change knowingly gives up.

#### `implemented/`

```markdown
## Problem
## Decision
…bespoke sections…
## Alternatives considered
## Consequences
```

`## Decision` describes shipped reality in the present tense, and the file is kept current with it. `## Consequences` records what the trade-off cost and bought. Proposal-era headings are spec-speak here and the gate rejects them: `## Proposal`, `## Plan`, `## Migration plan` and `## Acceptance criteria` may not appear in an implemented note. `## Testing`, `## Deferred` or `## Related` is fine where it states present-tense fact.

#### `rejected/`

A rejected note is the proposal, frozen: it keeps whatever proposal-time sections it had (including `## Acceptance criteria` or `## Plan`), and the verdict lives on the `Status:` line. Only the header block, the `## Problem` opener, a `## Proposal` section and the alternatives mandate apply.

### Alternatives considered — mandatory

Every note carries an `## Alternatives considered` section: each genuine alternative and why it lost, one bold-led paragraph per alternative or a `### Why not <X>?` subsection per contested one. A decision recorded without what it beat invites re-litigation — the failure notes exist to prevent.

Alternatives are recorded, never invented. For a corpus imported from an older format, a note dated before the project adopted this contract may carry this exact comment in place of the section when its alternatives are not reconstructible:

```markdown
<!-- agent-note-format: alternatives-not-recorded (pre-format Agent Note) -->
```

The comment is valid only for notes dated before the adoption date passed as `--format-adopted <yyyy-mm-dd>`; a note dated on or after that date always carries the section. Reconstructible alternatives are recorded rather than excused.

### Moving between lifecycles

Moving a file between lifecycle folders means updating the `Status:` line and re-satisfying that folder's skeleton in the same change — the gate fails the move otherwise. Concretely, `proposed/` → `implemented/` rewrites `## Proposal` into a present-tense `## Decision`, folds `## Acceptance criteria` and `## Risks` into `## Consequences` (or a present-tense `## Testing` or `## Verification` section for what now pins the behavior), and drops plans in favor of what shipped. It is the complete checkpoint: any unshipped accepted scope keeps the note `proposed/`. `proposed/` → `rejected/` only adds the reason to the `Status:` line and freezes the file.

### Companions

A note is the source member of a unit. The unit also contains every companion assigned to that note: translations, consistency records, diagrams or other supporting files. Repeated `--companion <suffix>` arguments classify same-stem companions. Repeated `--member <source>=<companion>` arguments declare exact membership when the mechanism uses another stem or nested path. Check paths are relative to the notes root; archive paths are relative to the archive root. A companion stays under the source's class, and an active member also stays under the same lifecycle. Neither form requires every note to have every possible companion. Notes are written for the agent in English; translations are optional reader companions.

An external mechanism owns a companion's naming convention, content, consistency records and validation. Agent Notes does not assume a translation format, target code, aggregate record or particular skill. The responsible model discovers the project's mechanism and resolves the current unit's members; the scripts receive those facts as parameters.

For a new note or a first seal unit, choose its translated target set in this order:

1. The current request's explicit choice.
2. An existing persistent project instruction.
3. The consistent target set of complete pairs in the same owner-defined class.
4. The primary agent's user language, when it differs from the source language.
5. No translated target.

Matching siblings, comparable classes and user language are model judgments, not CLI inference. A target set may contain several languages; every selected target becomes a unit member. Missing evidence, conflicting sibling target sets, an unavailable mechanism or an unknown user language selects no translated target without asking for a default. Installing a mechanism does not by itself enable translation for a project.

An existing translation workflow may require separate production and review. If that separation is unavailable, do not translate in the working context: keep the source note, report the selected targets as pending unit members, and hand over the missing mechanism with a resumable next step.

Target migration is asymmetric by cost. Adding a target is progressive: a new note receives the current target set, an edited existing note adds its missing targets, and an untouched note remains unchanged. Removing a target is consistent across every eligible active and unsealed unit. A sealed unit is historical evidence and never gains or loses a member. Range operations that inspect or record existing units do not create missing targets.

Companions form one unit with their note: they are moved, sealed and deleted together. The format gate reports a suffix-classified companion without a source and validates every path-scoped member source and companion as regular, contained files. The owning mechanism checks internal consistency. Seal preparation records the exact members expected for each new unit; seal-time completeness applies that unit's expected set, not a global target union. Verification does not replay the expectation over frozen history.

## Pruning the active tree

Judge every note semantically; word count and age are discovery aids, never criteria.

- **Implemented — delete:** delete complete units that only describe small presentation adjustments or purely mechanical changes, and repair or remove inbound links. A local bug fix, performance change, new capability, or substantive behavior or ownership decision does not qualify merely because its implementation is small.
- **Implemented — keep:** retain a note when its rationale, alternatives, negative guarantees, durable or wire semantics, ownership boundary, security rule, or reintroduction condition is likely to guide a future change. Classify the decision, not the mechanics of its implementation: a mechanical rename or type extraction can still record a lasting naming, compatibility or ownership rule.
- **Implemented — archive:** move a substantive historical decision to [the archive](archive-contract.md) when it is complete and unlikely to guide future work but its historical rationale still warrants preservation.
- **Proposed — never archive:** keep a live proposal active; if it is no longer worth pursuing, reject it with an honest reason and satisfy the rejected lifecycle format.

A long export loses all progress when the process stops. Users need to resume without rebuilding work that was already saved.

Checkpoint writes can contend with concurrent resume attempts, and cancellation cleanup can fail after the process loses access to temporary storage.

# Translating paired documents

## Invocation boundary

This skill runs when a persistent project instruction, the user or the responsible workflow selects an existing or new pair for creating, updating or checking, or when a documented change touches either side of an existing pair. An explicit `--require-target` may apply the project's declared completeness policy to a selected source set. It does not activate for ordinary one-off translation, an unpaired document's edit, or an inferred translation need that supplies no pair scope. Those sources authorize creating or updating a pair; once selected, translation and pairing are required, and failure is handed off unfinished. Installation alone is not activation. The [pairing contract](references/pairing-contract.md) owns path scope, target-selection rules and failure details.

## Defaults

Apply this skill's use-site default only when neither the request nor existing project instructions choose one. Treat existing instructions as authoritative read-only input; do not ask for, create, modify, or copy instructions merely to select a default.

## What this skill is

A self-contained mechanism for a corpus of paired Markdown documents: the skill entry, three references, and one bundled script. `<skill-dir>` is the directory containing this `SKILL.md`; run the script from the project root. The script is parameter-driven; the pairing contract owns the options, their defaults and the override rules. The check verifies existing pairs by default: file structure, Markdown structure, generated-region equality and the recorded hashes. It does not decide independently that a source should have a counterpart; that decision belongs to the standing instructions, the user, or the workflow responsible for the document scope and reaches the command as an explicit `--require-target`.

## Choose targets

The responsible model or workflow resolves a target set for each source in this order:

1. the current request;
2. an existing persistent project instruction;
3. complete pairs in the same owner-defined class or scope;
4. the primary agent's known user language;
5. no target.

The script receives the resulting explicit `--target` values and never infers from sibling files or the user's language. An explicit set may contain multiple targets. Do not choose a target when complete peer pairs disagree or the only candidate equals the source language.

Adding a target is progressive: a new source uses the current policy set, while an edited source adds only its missing targets. Untouched sources are not backfilled. A target added to an existing source uses the whole-document path because it has no confirmed state.

Removing a target is a strong cleanup across every eligible active source: remove its counterparts, switcher entries and record entries. Frozen or excluded documents stay unchanged. Report every unfinished source rather than claiming the scope completed.

## The pairing model

A pair is a source `foo.md`, one counterpart per target `foo.zh.md` or `foo.<lang>.md`, and one aggregate record `foo.i18n.yaml`. The [pairing contract](references/pairing-contract.md) owns the record and signature format, switchers, selection, regions, links, terminology, the CLI's options/defaults/exit codes and discovery prunes; the [style examples](references/style-examples.md) file carries the default voice guidance and samples. The script is `<skill-dir>/scripts/translate-pair.mjs`; its verbs are `list`, `check`, `write`, `brief` (with `--apply`), `init`, and `region render|splice`.

## Triage by change type

- **Existing pair, small local change** (one or two Markdown units in one section; no new or moved terminology, no structural change, no generated region): update the counterpart directly on the spot. This is the lightweight path.
- **Existing pair, any other change**: the briefing path.
- **New pair** (standing instructions, explicit instruction or authorization from the responsible workflow): the whole-document path and its isolation rule.
- **New target on an existing source** (progressive policy addition): the whole-document path for that target, while existing targets follow their normal update path.
- **Deleted or renamed document**: follow § Finish the pair; a named `write --target` never drops a target, and an entry without a counterpart is an incomplete pair.
- **Generated region**: the generator updates both sides; never edit a region by hand.
- **Frozen or excluded document**: the standing instructions say it is not maintained; do not create, update or repair its pairs.
- **Locale-selected detail page**: when the project selects the page by locale metadata and publishes no in-document switcher or record, declare its localized paths with `--unpaired <glob>`; the paths stay outside pair discovery and existing-target inference, links to different localized versions still normalize to one semantic target, and their locale differences are not violations. The project's link, prose and review checks keep both localized versions in step.

Every successful update path continues with § Finish the pair.

## Preserve working separation

The briefing and whole-document paths preserve a prose translator's independence. Use an isolated subagent when available; otherwise use a clean-context handoff, staged independent review, or another verifiable mechanism that preserves the separation. If no mechanism preserves it, follow § Stop and hand over rather than continuing in the working context.

## The lightweight update path

Use it only when the change is local (one or two Markdown units in one section), the terminology table already covers the touched terms and no first occurrence moves, no heading, list, table or fence structure changes, and no generated region is involved. Then:

1. Load the target's terminology table, or run `init` first when it is missing. Read the style guidance from the project's declared style file, or the default [style examples](references/style-examples.md) when none is declared; consult the nearest sample only when the touched wording needs calibration.
2. Make the smallest counterpart edit that covers the change; preserve the reviewed phrasing of everything untouched. Do not re-read or re-translate the whole document.
3. Follow the [translation rules](references/translation-rules.md); calibrate against the nearest declared/default sample when the wording needs it.

When more than one target exists and the wording of each is more than a local patch, use the briefing path per target. If the change turns out to cross sections, need a terminology decision, or alter structure, stop and use the briefing path instead.

## The briefing path

1. **Brief the change.** `node <skill-dir>/scripts/translate-pair.mjs brief <pair path> --target <lang>` prints the authored side's change since the last confirmed state at the narrowest aligned unit, with three-way text, matching terminology rows and first-occurrence notes. Generated regions never enter the briefing: aligned regeneration says nothing to brief; disagreeing current regions are a precondition failure. The pair must be committed.
2. **Apply a mechanical-only change directly.** When the brief maps every change inside fenced code, add `--apply`; the script splices and structure-validates the counterpart. On prose changes `--apply` exits 2 and writes nothing.
3. **Brief the prose translator.** Pass the briefing, or the command to print it, through the working separation in § Preserve working separation. The brief is the translator's change-local work set: it carries the diff, touched terminology and rules digest, but it does not replace the binding rules. Before editing, the translator reads the project's declared style file or the default references/style-examples.md; it also loads the target terminology table under the [translation rules](references/translation-rules.md). Escalate to the whole-document sources only when a decision is genuinely unanswerable.
4. Make the smallest edit that covers the change, then verify the changed spans against the source.

## The whole-document path

The translator reads the project's standing instructions, the [pairing contract](references/pairing-contract.md), the [translation rules](references/translation-rules.md), the project's declared style file or the default [style examples](references/style-examples.md) first; when the target's terminology table is missing, run `node <skill-dir>/scripts/translate-pair.mjs init --target <lang>=<name>` first. Translate the whole file section by section, keeping each section's structure locked to the source.

### Translate

- **Pass 1 — write, don't transpose.** Read a semantic unit, then restate it as a native technical author; preserve the frame without sentence-by-sentence correspondence.
- **Pass 2 — verify against the source, clause by clause.** Nothing added or dropped; every term follows the table; every code span survived verbatim. Fix by rewriting natively.
- **Read the completed counterpart alone.** Rewrite phrasing whose awkwardness only appears in isolation.
- Write only the final text, never drafts or notes.
- Never edit a generated region; the generator writes both sides.

A generated source (`--generated`) omits only its own switcher; the counterpart backlink remains required.

## Find the work

- `list` reports the pairs that exist; use `--select <glob>` and `--skip <glob>` to narrow the set, and `--unpaired <glob>` to exclude locale-selected pages from pairing. `--require-target <lang>` applies a declared full-pair policy to the selected sources and reports missing targets.
- `brief` with no pair argument reports every drifted existing pair; a pair it cannot brief is reported on stderr, the other briefs are still emitted without `--apply`, and the command exits 2. A generated-region drift is fatal for the whole run.
- Discovery walks hidden directories and applies the [pairing contract's default prune trees](references/pairing-contract.md#discovery). Frozen or vendored trees are kept out of the work by the standing instructions and the selection filters.
- In a change that edits a paired document, the work list is the change's diff: every changed side needs its counterpart brought along and the pair recorded in the same change.
- A source-side change is reflected in every existing target pair of that source in the same change. A translation-only correction that leaves the source untouched stays pair-local.

## Finish the pair

1. A new pair or whole-document translation carries the source and counterpart switcher lines; a generated source omits only its own switcher. Regenerate generated regions on both sides; they are not translated.
2. Edit a target, then run `write --target`; never write before editing. When several targets change, edit and write each target sequentially, then run `write --all` once after all targets are updated so the aggregate record is refreshed in one render. Never hand-edit the aggregate record; the script writes it. The record diff is the reviewable statement that the sides match.
3. When a source and its pairs are deleted, delete them together: the source, every counterpart, the aggregate record and inbound links. When a source is renamed, move the source, its counterparts and record to the new stem, repair their switchers and inbound links, then run `write --all` for the renamed source. When only a target is retired, leave the source in place, remove that counterpart and its switcher entry, and run `write --all` for the source; when the last target is removed, that command removes the empty aggregate record. A named `write --target` never retires a target.
4. Do not widen the work beyond the documents selected by the project instructions, the user or the responsible workflow.
5. Before handing over, the touched pairs are green under `check`, and a range-wide run checks every existing pair the change touched (when available, use the `dsh-spec-pre-push-checks` skill). Report the exact `write` and `check` commands and their observed results.
6. Keep the handover reviewable: say which pairs are new, which were minimally updated, and list pending terms and terminology decisions prominently.

## Responding to translation review

Follow the project's review-reporting convention (when available, use the `dsh-spec-code-review` skill). Evaluate each comment on its merits. A terminology comment is a decision about the project's terminology table, not about one file: apply the decided rendering through the project's procedure, and to the pair it came from.

## Stop and hand over

Stop and report instead of guessing when:

- the pair's last-confirmed state cannot be recovered, or a minimal update is named for an incomplete pair;
- the change would need a terminology decision the table does not make;
- the two sides' generated regions disagree, or a generated source is not declared;
- the target's terminology table is missing and `init` cannot create it because the target language is undeclared or its display name is neither declared nor learnable from the counterpart or the standing instructions;
- a structural change cannot be mapped safely;
- the prose-briefing or whole-document path cannot preserve the required working separation through an isolated subagent, a clean-context handoff, a staged independent review, or another verifiable mechanism;

and hand the change to review with the missing mechanism, completed work, pending work, pairs, records, unresolved decisions, and the resumable next step named.

# Pairing contract

The rules the skill's script enforces and the workflow follows. The check verifies **existing
pairs** by default; creation and update are driven by the project's standing instructions, the
user's instruction, or the workflow responsible for the source's document scope. A project whose
policy requires every selected source to carry a target passes `--require-target <lang>` to turn
that declared completeness policy into missing-pair violations.

The responsible model or workflow resolves the target set and supplies it through explicit
`--target` values. The script never infers a target from a sibling file, operating-system locale or
the primary agent's user language. An explicit set may contain multiple targets; every selected
target must be completed. Once selected, translation and pairing are required work, and failure
remains an incomplete handoff.

## The pair

A pair is:

- a source document `foo.md`, with no language suffix;
- one counterpart per target: `foo.zh.md` for the default target, `foo.<lang>.md` otherwise;
- one **aggregate** record for the source: `foo.i18n.yaml`, holding every target language.

A source may have counterparts in any subset of the declared targets; different sources may carry
different target sets. Completeness is explicit: without `--require-target`, an absent artifact
does not create a required pair.

### Target selection and change

The responsible workflow resolves a target set for one source in this order:

1. the current request;
2. an existing persistent project instruction;
3. complete pairs in the same owner-defined class or scope;
4. the primary agent's known user language;
5. no target.

Use peer pairs only as evidence for that source's default. A conflicting peer set, an unknown user
language or a candidate equal to the source language selects no default target. Do not ask merely
to replace a default.

Target addition is progressive. A new source uses the current policy set; an existing source gains
missing targets only when its content changes. Untouched sources are not backfilled. A target added
to an existing source starts from the whole-document path because that target has no
last-confirmed state.

Target removal is a strong cleanup across the eligible active scope. Remove the counterparts,
switcher entries and aggregate-record entries, and report unfinished sources individually. Frozen
or excluded documents remain unchanged. These rules define an end state; they do not require a
range mutation to be one filesystem transaction.

The source language is a property of the source file: it is the code on the source hash line
of every record section once one exists. When the first record is written it is supplied with
`--source-lang <code>[=<display>]`, defaulting to `en` only when the flag is omitted; the record
stores the code and never the display. A source filename must not carry a target suffix;
`foo.fr.md` is the fr target's counterpart, not a source. Mixed source languages are created by
writing each source separately, not by one `write --all` command.

The mechanical default target is `zh` (display name `中文`) when `--target` is omitted. It is not
an inference from project context. An explicit non-default target must carry a display name
(`--target ja=日本語`); `--target zh` alone resolves to `中文`.

## The record

One aggregate record per source, flat: every section has one source hash line and one target
signature line per target. No nested blocks and no per-target source version.

    # Pairing consistency record for guide.md (references/pairing-contract.md): per heading
    # source hash plus one target signature per target; a target signature binds the source hash.
    # Re-record with:
    #   node <skill-dir>/scripts/translate-pair.mjs write docs/guide.md --target <lang>
    /guide:
      fr: 41d772192075e133
      ja: 0b7d5e4f8a9c1d2e
      zh: dda91c6c670cfd9d

- H(source, target) is SHA-256 over the UTF-8 string source + a newline + target, truncated to the
  first 16 hexadecimal characters. source and target are the 16-hex content hashes of the two
  sides. A recorded target signature is H(sourceHash, targetContentHash), so it binds the exact
  source version it was confirmed against.
- A section's content hash covers its translated blocks, excluding fenced code and generated
  regions; a section with no translated content on either side has no entry.
- The canonical comment and blank lines are ignored when the check compares the body; body order
  and formatting are enforced. Section order is the current source document's heading order;
  sections no longer present are dropped. Canonical body order is the source hash line first
  (keyed by the source language code), then target signature lines sorted by target code.
- Section keys are heading paths; repeated paths get ~2, ~3, ... in document order.
- write --target <lang> updates the source hash line and only that target's signature. If the
  source changed, the other targets' signatures are bound to the earlier source and the check
  reports them out of sync; they are not silently confirmed. Translating targets one at a time is
  supported: edit a counterpart, write --target, then continue with the next; untouched targets
  stay red until written. Writing a target before editing it confirms the unchanged content, so
  write only after the edit. Concurrent writes for one source are read-modify-write races; run them
  sequentially.
- write --all updates every existing target signature of the selected source in one render and
  drops a recorded target whose counterpart is gone. When the last target is dropped the record
  file is removed. A named write --target never drops a target.
- A target counterpart without a target signature line, or a target signature line without a
  counterpart, is an incomplete pair for that target.
- The record path is always foo.i18n.yaml; there is no per-target record file.
- The record is generated. Do not hand-edit it; write is the only record mutation. write --all is
  the migration path: it replaces an old or unreadable record body for a selected source by
  rendering the current aggregate record, while a named write --target refuses a malformed record.

## Selection, arguments and empty results

Named arguments:

| Argument | Selects |
|---|---|
| `foo.md` or `foo` | every target that has a counterpart or a record entry for the source; `--target` narrows |
| `foo.zh.md` | that target's pair |
| `foo.i18n.yaml` | every target of that source that has a record entry; `--target` narrows |

A named source selects only its own counterpart files and record entries, or the target named with
`--target`, never a target inferred from a sibling counterpart file; a non-default target with no
artifact of its own needs `--target <lang>`.

`--select <glob>` and `--skip <glob>` narrow a corpus-wide run by source path; they never change
link normalization. `--require-target <lang>` adds an explicit declared-completeness demand for
every selected source; it belongs to `check` and `list` and cannot be combined with named pairs.

Range `check`, `list`, `brief` and `write --all` never create missing targets. They inspect or
record existing pairs, so a policy that adds a target does not turn untouched sources into failed
or backfilled work.

Empty results by verb:

| Verb | No existing pair / no selection | Exit |
|---|---|---|
| `list` | report zero rows | 0 |
| `check` | "nothing to check is not a green check" | 2 |
| `check --require-target` | one or more selected sources lack the required counterpart | 1 |
| `write --all` | "nothing to record" | 1 |
| `write <pair>` | a named pair whose artifacts are all absent names no pair | 2 |
| `brief` (no pair, nothing drifted) | "nothing to brief" when pairs exist and all are consistent | 0 |
| `brief` (no pair, no pairs exist) | no pair to consider | 2 |
| `brief <pair>` consistent | a named pair is consistent | 2 |

A named pair with some artifacts present but a missing counterpart is incomplete: `check` exits 1,
`write` exits 2, `brief` exits 2. A corpus-wide `brief` emits the briefs it can compute, reports each pair it cannot brief on stderr, and exits 2; a named pair that cannot be briefed is a usage error, and a generated-region drift is fatal for the whole run. With `--apply`, a skipped pair means no briefing is printed and nothing is written; skipped pairs are still reported on stderr, and the command exits 2. The script never reads a project config file; the standing instructions' facts arrive as flags.

## Language switchers

The switcher is the unique paragraph in the H1 section whose labels and links match the canonical
line. Position is free: a format-mandated `Status:` paragraph may precede it. The source side is

`<source label> | [<target label>](<counterpart path>) | ...`

listing every existing counterpart in language-code order; the counterpart side is

`[<source label>](<source path>) | <target label>`.

- A destination is the relative counterpart path or an absolute URL whose pathname ends with that
  repository-relative path.
- A declared target pins its label; an undeclared existing target's label is learned from its
  counterpart's trailing text.
- The source label is learned from the counterpart backlink. The write-only --source-lang display
  is not stored and does not pin it; the counterpart's link label is authoritative.
- Zero matches, two matches, a wrong label, an extra link or an inline-code quote are violations.
- Only the matched switcher paragraph's links are exempt from the signature and locale checks.
- A source declared with `--generated <glob>` waives only its own switcher; the counterpart
  backlink is still required.

## Structure and links

The check compares the two sides' structural signature: heading depths and order, fenced code
bytes, table row and column counts, list kinds, ordered-list starts and item counts, and semantic
link targets. Paragraph order, inline emphasis and prose wording are review's domain.

Paired-document links normalize to one semantic target. Resolve a destination to its base source
path. A destination selected by `--unpaired` still normalizes to that base, so different localized
versions compare as one semantic target, but its locale difference is not a violation and it stays
outside pair discovery and existing-target inference. Every other destination enters normalization
when its base has at least one counterpart file or any aggregate record entry. `--select`/`--skip`
do not affect this predicate. Adding or removing a pair changes normalization for links that point
at it, so affected existing pairs must be re-recorded in the same change.

## Generated regions

The marker shell follows the upstream shape; the layout rules are this skill's:

```markdown
<!-- BEGIN GENERATED config-catalog:@scope/package -->
| ... |
<!-- END GENERATED config-catalog:@scope/package -->
```


- BEGIN and END occupy their own line at column 0. The exact shell is
  `^<!-- BEGIN GENERATED (\S+)(?: [^>]*)? -->$` for BEGIN and
  `^<!-- END GENERATED (\S+) -->$` for END: the slug is one non-whitespace
  token, BEGIN may carry a trailing note, END may not. A line that starts like a marker after
  optional leading whitespace or an inline comment but does not parse as one is a malformed marker.
- A marker must be its own block: blank lines or document boundaries around the region as a whole;
  region content may abut its markers.
- Markers inside fenced code are ordinary code, including a fenced marker sample inside a region.
- Nested BEGIN, END without BEGIN, slug mismatch, an unclosed BEGIN, a duplicate slug in one file,
  a malformed marker-shaped line, a marker inside a list or paragraph, and a marker-shaped line
  inside a region's content are violations.
- Before sectioning, structure-signature computation and record hashing, every region line is
  replaced by spaces of the same length; line numbering and offsets are preserved. A generated
  heading therefore never creates a section, signature entry, locale violation or record input.
- Both sides' regions must have the same slugs, order and content after paired-document link
  normalization, and each region must sit under the same authored section on both sides (the
  nearest preceding authored heading's ordinal; a region before the first heading has ordinal 0).
  A mismatch says "regenerate both sides".
- Regenerating both sides changes neither the record nor the section keys. A briefing excludes
  regions: aligned regeneration says nothing to brief; disagreeing current regions are a
  precondition failure.
- Only the generator edits a region. The skill exposes `region render` and `region splice` as a
  correctness-enforcing CLI for generators; it exposes no JavaScript generator API. `render --slug
<slug> --body <file|->` prints the two marker lines and the body, validated against the shell and
  rejecting a body that contains a marker-shaped line. `splice <file> --slug <slug> --body
<file|->` requires the file to contain exactly one region with that slug, replaces only that
  region, validates the whole resulting document against the marker grammar (own block, fence,
  duplicate slug, unclosed), and writes only on success. It never creates, moves, inserts or removes
  a region; zero or multiple matches exit 2, as does an invalid body.

## Discovery

The script walks the repository from its root, entering hidden directories, skipping `.git` and
symlinks, and matching `.md` and `.i18n.yaml` files. The default prune trees are:

`node_modules`, `vendor`, `dist`, `build`, `out`, `target`, `coverage`, `__pycache__`,
`.venv`, `.cache`, `.pnpm-store`, `.agents/skills`, `.agents/dsh-spec-translate-docs`.

A bare prune name matches a directory at any depth. A frozen or vendored tree is kept out of the
work by the standing instructions and `--skip`; it is not a corpus exclusion state.

Some products publish locale-selected detail pages outside the paired-document corpus. When the
project maps such a document by locale metadata and its pages carry no in-document switcher or
consistency record, pass every localized path through `--unpaired <glob>`. Those paths are excluded
from pair discovery and existing-target inference, while links to their different localized
versions still normalize to one semantic target and their locale differences are not violations.
The project's link, prose and review checks still keep the localized versions in step.

## Project data

- **Terminology.** Default root `.agents/dsh-spec-translate-docs/`; default files `terminology.md`
  for the default target and `terminology.<lang>.md` for another target. `--terminology
  <lang>=<path>` overrides the path; location and naming are otherwise the project's. The table
  format is fixed: source term, target rendering, first-occurrence form, forbidden renderings, note.
  `init` writes the template for one target and never overwrites an existing file. `brief` requires
  the target's table and exits 2 with the init hint when it is missing.
- **Style.** [style-examples.md](style-examples.md) is the skill's default style file: guidance plus reviewed English-to-Chinese samples, read before every translation including a lightweight update. The project's standing instructions may name its own style file in any location or format; that file replaces the default whole file. The binding priority lives in [translation rules](translation-rules.md); the style file points to it. No project path is required and the script never reads style files.

## The script

Verbs:

| Verb | What it does |
|---|---|
| `list` | report existing pairs as `ok`, `out-of-sync` or `missing`; exit 0 |
| `check [pairs]` | verify named pairs or every existing pair; 0 clean, 1 violations, 2 usage or empty selection |
| `write [pairs] \| --all` | recompute the selected targets' recorded hashes; `--all` also drops recorded targets whose counterpart is gone; 0 written, 1 nothing to record, 2 a named pair is incomplete or a record is malformed |
| `brief [pairs]` | print the minimal-update briefing; `--apply` for a code-fence-only change; 0 nothing to brief, 1 the mechanical splice would violate structure, 2 a precondition |
| `init` | write one target's terminology template; 0 created or already exists, 2 usage |
| `region render --slug <slug> --body <file\|->` | print a marker-delimited region |
| `region splice <file> --slug <slug> --body <file\|->` | replace the one existing region and validate the whole file; 0 written, 2 usage or validation |

Shared options: `--target <lang>[=<display>]` (repeatable), `--require-target <lang>[=<display>]`
(`check`/`list`), `--source-lang <code>[=<display>]`
(write only, first record; the code is stored, the display is not), `--select <glob>`,
`--skip <glob>`, `--unpaired <glob>`, `--generated <glob>`, `--terminology <lang>=<path>`, `--root <dir>`,
and the verb-specific `--apply` and `--all`.

Exit codes are 0 (clean or written), 1 (violations or nothing to record) and 2 (usage or a
precondition). A failed write, splice or `--apply` writes nothing.

## What the check decides, and what review owns

The check decides: pair completeness for the selected targets, recorded hashes matching current
content, canonical record body, switchers, structural signature, generated-region equality and
section anchors, generated-source exemption and link locale. It does not decide translation
quality, terminology choice, list or table order, noncanonical numbering, inline code, emphasis,
meaning or tone; review owns those. A green check means the pair was confirmed consistent at these
exact contents, not that the confirmation was sound.
